newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: WELFARE PROPOSED FOR S.AFRICA'S POOREST CHILDREN.
newsitem.headline: WELFARE PROPOSED FOR S.AFRICA'S POOREST CHILDREN.

text.p: A South African government- appointed committee on Wednesday recommended sweeping changes to the state's 1.2 billion rand a year child support system to spread the benefit to black children excluded under apartheid.

"A few people who got it all will get a lot less. A lot of people who got nothing will get a little more. It is inevitably going to be controversial," committee chairwoman Francie Lund told a news conference.
The 12-member committee proposed a flat-rate child subsidy of 70 or 125 rand a month for each child aged up to four, six or nine years payable to parents unable to care for their own children.
The grant would be paid quarterly to limit the distribution costs and would be linked to a modest health-care programme and proper birth registration.
The proposals would cost between 1.2 billion rand, the current national budget for child support, and two billion rand a year, depending on which option is chosen.
At present, a single parent not able to support his or her children can qualify for a 430 rand-a-month parent allowance and an additional 135 rand for each of up to two children.
"Though those who received the grants were poor, they did not go to all people who were poor. The African population has been effectively excluded from access," Lund said.
The committee calculated that extending the existing scheme to blacks would cost at least an additional five billion rand a year and possibly as much as 20 billion more.
"It is clear that if the proposals are accepted, there will be severe negative economic and social consequences for those on the present system.

"However, we believe that the proposals form the basis on which a sustainable, enduring and healthy lifeline can be given to many of the poorest South African children over the longer term," Lund said.
Welfare Minister Geraldine Fraser-Moleketi said she would study the report but warned it would not automatically be made government policy.
